commentary.seminaVerbi:
Elijah as “fire” reads like the psyche’s purgative force: the part of a person that refuses compromise with self-deception and therefore scorches the social order built on it. That refusal can look like famine and vengeance because it starves the old appetites; the violence is the image of inner detox, not mere cruelty. The whirlwind ascent is the fantasy of a life so integrated with its own imperative that it no longer needs ordinary continuity; it becomes pure trajectory, leaving a successor as the residue of its intensity.

The prayer’s insistence on few words is an attack on magical thinking: the anxious mind believes verbosity can purchase safety. “Father” names a trustful attachment stance; “hallowed” is the ego learning reverence for what it cannot control. “Forgive as you forgive” is psychological realism: resentment is a self-administered toxin, and the refusal to release another person keeps the self locked in the same punitive economy. “Lead us not into temptation” is the adult admission that willpower is finite and that environments, habits, and cues matter.

Semina Verbi: Elijah’s fiery purification parallels Shiva as destroyer of illusion in Shaivism, and the Taoist image of true power acting like a consuming clarity rather than coercion; speculation: the whirlwind resembles the shamanic ascent motif where the self is “taken” into a higher register to return as medicine. The short prayer echoes Zen’s suspicion of discursive grasping and the Sufi preference for dhikr that simplifies the heart; “forgive to be forgiven” meets Buddhist metta and the Stoic practice of releasing injury as a way to free one’s own ruling faculty.
commentary.excursus:
Sirach makes Elijah a pure instrument of appetite: fire that speaks, speech that burns. He doesn’t persuade; he reduces. Famine, lightning, kings snapped in half, the bed invaded. Holiness here is not gentleness but a kind of sanctioned violence, the pleasure of seeing power humiliated and the world made small enough to obey. Even his “friendship” is a dangerous honor, proximity to a man who can call down weather.

Then Matthew turns and forbids the very thing Elijah embodies: incantation, volume, the fantasy that enough words can bend heaven. The Lord’s Prayer is not a spell but a surrender, a tightening of desire into a few hard asks: bread, release, rescue. Yet the catch is psychological and brutal: forgiveness is not a virtue but a gate that only opens from inside. If you cling to your grievance, you lock yourself out and call it justice.

Read together, Elijah is the dream of external control—make the sky comply, make enemies vanish—while the prayer drags the battlefield inward. The real famine is the one you feed with resentment. The real fire is the one you keep rehearsing in your mouth. God already knows; the prayer is for you, to stop enjoying your wrath long enough to be delivered from it.
commentary.synthesis: God’s word governs history through appointed servants, and God’s prayer governs the petitioner by binding divine pardon to human pardon.

gospel.text: The prayer is structured as a reordering of loyalties: name, kingdom, will precede any petition, and the final plea concerns moral vulnerability rather than circumstance. The appended condition on forgiveness makes the prayer juridical: it binds the petitioner to the very mercy invoked.

reading.text: The passage constructs Elijah as a public instrument of divine governance: scarcity, judgment, and reversal of royal security are presented as the Lord’s enforcement executed through a man. The repeated “who…” is a litany of delegated authority, culminating in a role that exceeds his lifetime.

Elijah is framed as eschatological function: “registered” for appointed times, tasked with turning hearts and restoring tribes. Yet the same spirit is said to be “filled up” in Elisha, making continuity—not nostalgia—the point: the office persists by transmission.

marginalia.text: Prophet as combustion: person becomes element; speech becomes flame.
Heaven “shut up”: drought as liturgical censure; fire answers fire.
Resurrection is attributed to “word,” not technique; command outruns death’s allotment.
Ascent is not escape but translation: fire carries fire.
Corpse still speaks: prophecy outlives breath; death fails to silence office.
Prayer is not verbosity; pagan logic treats God as a mechanism to be triggered.
Foreknowledge of need strips prayer of informing; it becomes alignment, not briefing.
Bread named beyond substance: request is for a life that exceeds calories.
Debt-language: sin is obligation incurred; forgiveness is release, not amnesia.
Refusal to forgive installs a closed circuit: you keep what you demand to be remitted.

hoursOfPrayer.prayer: O God, the strength of those who hope in you, hear our supplications, and since man is frail and without you can do nothing, grant us the help of your grace, that we may keep your commandments and please you in our actions and desires. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God for ever and ever.
hoursOfPrayer.label: Matins

hoursOfPrayer.prayer: Almighty and eternal God: enlighten with your light the peoples who live in darkness and in the shadow of death, for by that light the Dayspring from on high has visited us, Jesus Christ our Lord. Who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God for ever and ever.
hoursOfPrayer.label: Lauds

hoursOfPrayer.prayer: Lord, you who at the hour of Terce sent the Holy Spirit upon the apostles gathered in prayer, grant that we too may share in the gifts of this Spirit. Through Jesus Christ our Lord.
hoursOfPrayer.label: Terce

hoursOfPrayer.prayer: Almighty and eternal God, before you there is neither darkness nor gloom; therefore let the brightness of your light shine upon us, so that, keeping your commandments, we may walk faithfully in your ways with hearts enlarged. Through Jesus Christ our Lord.
hoursOfPrayer.label: Sext

hoursOfPrayer.prayer: Look upon your family at prayer, Lord, and grant that, by imitating the examples of patience of your Son, it may never lose heart in adversity. Through Jesus Christ our Lord.
hoursOfPrayer.label: Nones

hoursOfPrayer.prayer: Almighty God, we give you thanks for the day now ending and implore your mercy, that you may graciously forgive us all the faults which, through the frailty of the human condition, we have committed this day. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever.
hoursOfPrayer.label: Vespers

hoursOfPrayer.prayer:
Let us pray:
Lord our God, grant us a peaceful rest that restores our strength, now worn down by the day’s work; so that, strengthened by your help, we may always serve you with our whole body and spirit. Through Jesus Christ our Lord.
hoursOfPrayer.label: Compline

lines: And Elias the prophet stood up, as a fire, and his word burnt like a torch.
He brought a famine upon them, and they that provoked him in their envy, were reduced to a small number, for they could not endure the commandments of the Lord.
By the word of the Lord he shut up the heaven, and he brought down fire from heaven thrice.
Thus was Elias magnified in his wondrous works. And who can glory like to thee?
Who raisedst up a dead man from below, from the lot of death, by the word of the Lord God.
Who broughtest down kings to destruction, and brokest easily their power in pieces, and the glorious from their bed.
Who heardest judgment in Sina, and in Horeb the judgments of vengeance.
Who anointedst kings to penance, and madest prophets successors after thee.
Who wast taken up in a whirlwind of fire, in a chariot of fiery horses.
Who art registered in the judgments of times to appease the wrath of the Lord, to reconcile the heart of the father to the son, and to restore the tribes of Jacob.
Blessed are they that saw thee, and were honoured with thy friendship.
For we live only in our life, but after death our name shall not be such.
Elias was indeed covered with the whirlwind, and his spirit was filled up in Eliseus: in his days he feared not the prince, and no man was more powerful than he.
No word could overcome him, and after death his body prophesied.
readings.heading: A reading from the Book of Sirach

lines: And when you are praying, speak not much, as the heathens. For they think that in their much speaking they may be heard.
Be not you therefore like to them for your Father knoweth what is needful for you, before you ask him.
Thus therefore shall you pray: Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name.
Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven.

Give us this day our supersubstantial bread. Supersubstantial bread... In St. Luke the same word is rendered daily bread. It is understood of the bread of life, which we receive in the Blessed Sacrament.
And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.
And lead us not into temptation. But deliver us from evil. Amen. Lead us not into temptation... That is, suffer us not to be overcome by temptation.
For if you will forgive men their offences, your heavenly Father will forgive you also your offences.
But if you will not forgive men, neither will your Father forgive you your offences.
